prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Baidu, Inc." (ticker BIDU), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BIDU", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Baidu, Inc.
result.industry: Internet search, online advertising, AI cloud and autonomous driving
markets: China internet search and online advertising
AI cloud infrastructure and GPU cloud (Baidu AI Cloud)
Large language models and AI apps (ERNIE, Wenku, Netdisk)

mission.statement: to make the complicated world simpler through technology
mission.source: Company press releases, 'About Baidu' section (e.g. Baidu World 2021 release on baidu.gcs-web.com)
mission.plain: Use technology, especially AI, to make finding information and getting things done easier.

about.plain: Baidu runs China's biggest search engine, a bit like Google for China. It makes most of its money by showing ads next to search results and in its apps. It also rents out powerful computers for AI, builds its own AI chatbot called ERNIE, and runs driverless taxis called Apollo Go. It owns most of iQIYI, a video streaming service like Netflix.
about.customers: Businesses that buy ads and cloud computing from it, plus people who pay for iQIYI memberships and AI apps.
about.everyday: Hundreds of millions of people in China use the Baidu app to search, and some can hail a Baidu robotaxi with no driver in cities like Wuhan.

money.part: Traditional search and feed ads (legacy business)
money.plain: ads in search results and the Baidu app
renting GPU and AI computing power
subscriptions to AI tools like Wenku, Netdisk and ERNIE
ads built around AI agents and AI search answers

money.part: Apollo Go robotaxis and Kunlunxin AI chips
money.plain: driverless taxi rides and AI chips

result.summary: Baidu still dominates Chinese web search and owns valuable full-stack AI assets (Kunlun chips, AI cloud, ERNIE models, Apollo Go robotaxis), but its core moat is eroding as users shift to Douyin, WeChat and AI chatbots from ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent and DeepSeek. Revenue fell in 2024 and 2025 and the company took a RMB16.2 billion impairment on its core asset group in 2025, so its advantage is real but narrowing.

pricingPower.evidence: Total revenue fell 3% to RMB129.1 billion in 2025 and another 4% year over year in Q2 2026 as advertisers cut budgets and Baidu deliberately held back AI-search monetization; management expects ads to stay under pressure in H2 2026, and AI cloud competes in a price war with Alibaba, ByteDance and Tencent.

moats.evidence: 'Baidu it' is a verb for searching in China and Baidu still had the largest search share (46.65% on StatCounter), but younger users increasingly search inside Douyin, WeChat and AI chatbots.
Consumers can switch search or chatbot apps for free; some lock-in exists for Baidu AI Cloud enterprise customers and ad customers using its tools.

More searches and advertisers improve ad targeting and its content ecosystem (Baike, Zhidao, Wenku), and Apollo Go's 23 million+ cumulative rides feed its driving data, though walled gardens like WeChat cut it off from much content.
Baidu owns a full AI stack from Kunlun chips to cloud to models, letting it run large clusters partly on its own chips amid US export controls, but rivals Alibaba and ByteDance outspend it on capex.
Chinese search and cloud markets support several large players, and new AI entrants have entered easily.
Baidu is the incumbent being counter-positioned: AI answers cannibalize its own search-ad model, which is why it held back AI search monetization in 2026.
More than a decade of AI and autonomous-driving R&D (Apollo started in 2017) gives Baidu fully driverless robotaxi operations in multiple cities and one airbag deployment per 14.4 million km.
Its Kunlunxin chip unit is a scarce domestic AI-chip asset, but AI talent is widely poached by ByteDance, Alibaba and startups.

customers.evidence: ERNIE Assistant daily active users rose 83% year over year in Q2 2026, but Baidu's search app has lost user time to Douyin and Doubao, and its ad customers have been cutting spending (ads under pressure through 2026).

talent.evidence: Baidu was long called the 'Whampoa Military Academy' of China's AI talent, but many alumni left for ByteDance, Alibaba and startups, and it reorganized its model teams and added AI talent in 2026.

product.evidence: Apollo Go is among the world's largest robotaxi services (about 1 million fully driverless rides in Q2 2026, operations in Dubai and testing in London with Uber and Lyft) and Kunlun chips are competitive domestically, but ERNIE models trail DeepSeek, Qwen and Doubao in usage and benchmarks.

competitors.name: ByteDance (Douyin, Doubao, Volcano Engine)
competitors.note: Ad budgets, in-app search on Douyin, the Doubao chatbot and Volcano Engine AI cloud.

competitors.note: WeChat search, Yuanbao AI assistant, Tencent Cloud and ad budgets.

competitors.name: Alibaba Group
competitors.note: Alibaba Cloud (China's largest AI cloud), Qwen models and Quark AI search app.

competitors.name: DeepSeek
competitors.note: Open-source LLMs and chatbot competing with ERNIE.

competitors.name: Huawei (Huawei Cloud, Ascend)
competitors.note: AI cloud and Ascend AI chips competing with Baidu AI Cloud and Kunlunxin.

competitors.name: Kuaishou Technology
competitors.note: Online advertising budgets and Kling AI.

competitors.name: PDD Holdings
competitors.note: Merchant advertising budgets in e-commerce search.

competitors.name: Pony AI
competitors.note: Robotaxi services in Chinese cities and the Middle East.

competitors.name: WeRide
competitors.note: Robotaxi services, especially in Abu Dhabi and China.

competitors.name: Cambricon Technologies
competitors.note: Domestic AI accelerator chips competing with Kunlunxin.

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google, Waymo)
competitors.note: Search outside China and Waymo robotaxis in international markets.

estimates.name: Tencent Holdings (estimate; not an SEC filer)
Kuaishou Technology (estimate, FY2024; not an SEC filer)
Meituan (estimate, FY2024; not an SEC filer)

threats: Search usage shifting to Douyin, WeChat and AI chatbots (Doubao, Qwen, DeepSeek, Yuanbao), with online marketing revenue declining
AI answers cannibalizing search-ad revenue while Baidu holds back AI search monetization
Price war and heavy capex from Alibaba, ByteDance and Tencent in AI cloud
US chip export controls limiting access to Nvidia GPUs
Robotaxi regulation in Chinese cities (Q2 2026 ride volumes hit by operational adjustments) and competition from Pony AI, WeRide, Tesla and Waymo
US securities class action (class period Nov 18, 2025 to Aug 17, 2026) and US-China delisting or sanctions risk
Negative free cash flow from capex (RMB12.1 billion in 2025) while core profits fall

ceo.name: Robin Li (Li Yanhong)
ceo.background: Co-founder (2000); BS in information management from Peking University, MS in computer science from SUNY Buffalo; invented the RankDex hyperlink-analysis search algorithm

c1.evidence: Baidu leads China's robotaxi market with Apollo Go (23 million+ cumulative rides by June 2026) and is a top AI cloud player, but in its main AI-model and cloud markets Alibaba and ByteDance are larger.

c2.evidence: Users chose Baidu for being the default Chinese search engine with Chinese-language content (Baike, Zhidao), but that advantage is being copied away by Douyin, WeChat and AI chatbots, as 2025 revenue fell 3%.

c3.evidence: Baidu is a household name and the default search engine in China, but it is little known outside China and its search product has a weak reputation among users for ad clutter.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to make the complicated world simpler through technology' and long AI push are consistent, but past scandals over paid medical ads (Wei Zexi, 2016) undercut the purpose-over-money image.

c6.evidence: “search engine, ads, AI, robotaxi”: Chinese users see it as the old search leader with too many ads and a reputation hurt by the 2016 medical-ad scandal, while investors see it as an AI and robotaxi pioneer, so the impression is mixed.

c7.evidence: AI cloud, AI applications and autonomous driving are large, fast-growing markets; Baidu's AI Cloud Infra revenue grew 50% and GPU cloud revenue 283% year over year in Q2 2026.

c8.evidence: Baidu is expanding into AI cloud, Kunlun AI chips (M100, M300), AI agents and robotaxis in Dubai, Hong Kong, London and Switzerland.

m1.evidence: Robin Li bet on AI around 2017 (“All in AI”) and launched ERNIE Bot in March 2023, ahead of most Chinese peers.

m2.evidence: Robin Li co-founded Baidu in 2000 and has run it as CEO since 2004, controlling its strategy for over two decades.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence either way of servant-style leadership at Baidu.

m5.evidence: Baidu built a strong engineering and research culture (Baidu Research, Apollo, PaddlePaddle), but critics say it has been slow to turn research into hit products against ByteDance.

m6.evidence: Robin Li is a computer scientist who invented the RankDex search algorithm and personally presents Baidu's AI products at Baidu World.

m7.evidence: Li advocates AI for public good and served as a CPPCC member, but Baidu's past paid-medical-ad scandal raised questions about putting profit first.

m7b.evidence: No verified commencement speech by Robin Li at Stanford, Harvard or MIT was found.

m8b.evidence: Li is a well-known tech figure in China (famously doused with water on stage in 2018) but is reserved compared with Elon Musk or Alex Karp.

m9.evidence: He built China's dominant search engine and early AI and robotaxi leadership, but revenue has fallen since 2023 (RMB134.6 billion to RMB129.1 billion in 2025) and Baidu lost ground to ByteDance and Alibaba.

m10.evidence: Baidu is not specifically known for frugality, though it cut SG&A by 23% year over year in Q2 2026.

c10.evidence: Baidu search, maps and Netdisk serve hundreds of millions of people in China, but its products are rarely used outside China.

p2.evidence: Building frontier LLMs, AI chips under export controls and fully driverless robotaxis (about 1 million driverless rides in Q2 2026) is extremely hard and important.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in 2021 (RMB124.5 billion) and 2023 (RMB134.6 billion) but fell in 2022 (RMB123.7 billion), 2024 (RMB133.1 billion) and 2025 (RMB129.1 billion).

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 48.5% in 2020 to 43.9% in 2025 and operating margin from 13.4% to -4.5% after a RMB16.2 billion impairment.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Baidu had RMB283.1 billion in cash and investments versus about RMB103.9 billion of loans and notes, with total equity of RMB281.4 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from RMB14.3 billion in 2020 to a RMB5.8 billion loss in 2025, and operating cash flow from RMB24.2 billion to negative RMB3.0 billion.

v1.evidence: Baidu's search and ERNIE products are not clearly the best; many Chinese users prefer Doubao, DeepSeek or searching within Douyin and WeChat.

v2.evidence: Baidu has been a prestigious AI employer in China but no longer ranks among the most sought-after tech employers, with ByteDance and Alibaba attracting more AI talent.

c5.evidence: Chinese users and advertisers would miss Baidu search, Maps, Netdisk and Wenku, and robotaxi riders in Wuhan would miss Apollo Go, but close substitutes exist for most of them.
